# Ranga Reddy

> Hands-on notes, production troubleshooting and interactive tools for Apache Hudi, Iceberg, Spark, Kafka and the lakehouse stack underneath them.

Deep technical posts on Apache Spark, Hudi, Iceberg, XTable and the lakehouse
stack. Claims in these posts are verified by running them against real clusters
rather than recalled, and each post states the exact version it was tested on.

Author: Ranga Reddy. Canonical site: https://rangareddy.github.io/
Full index: https://rangareddy.github.io/sitemap.xml
Feed: https://rangareddy.github.io/feed.xml

If you quote from a post, link to the post URL listed below. Each entry is
`title: description` followed by the URL it lives at.

## Hudi

- [Hudi Merge-on-Read: the write you skipped, and the read that pays for it](https://rangareddy.github.io/HudiMergeOnRead/): Merge-on-Read is what lets a Hudi table accept a write every minute without rewriting a Parquet file each time. Here is where that saved work goes: what a file slice is, what is really inside a log file, who runs compaction, and what each of the three query types returns. Written against the latest Hudi release, 1.2.0 as of now.
- [Spark and Hudi logging: making a write explain itself](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkHudiCustomLogging/): A Hudi write that fails or drags leaves hundreds of log lines and almost no answer. Here is which Hudi loggers actually fire, the Log4j 2 config that keeps the five that matter, and how to read the instant lifecycle they print.
- [Apache Hudi architecture: what actually happens when you upsert a row](https://rangareddy.github.io/ApacheHudiArchitecture/): A walk through the Hudi runtime from a MERGE statement down to bytes on object storage: how a key finds its file group, which write handle runs, what the timeline records, and what a reader has to reconcile.
- [The Hudi index: how one lookup decides the cost of every upsert](https://rangareddy.github.io/HudiIndexTypes/): The index decides which file group an incoming record belongs to, which makes it the biggest lever you have on upsert cost. Hudi offers ten index types, including a partition-scoped record index that is cheaper than the global one for most partitioned tables. Here is how to pick.
- [Apache Hudi on Spark: the complete cheat sheet](https://rangareddy.github.io/ApacheHudiCheatSheet/): One page to keep open while you work: table types, file layout, the timeline, writer properties, key generators, query types, indexes, the metadata table, concurrency, schema evolution, table services, procedures and tuning, with the config key and default for each.
- [Apache Hudi: an introduction to its architecture, features and what makes it different](https://rangareddy.github.io/ApacheHudiGuide/): A foundations-to-production guide to Apache Hudi, covering what it is, the primitives it is built from, how a write and a read actually work, and the capabilities that exist in Hudi and nowhere else, including the record-level index, the multi-modal index, incremental queries and non-blocking concurrency.

## Iceberg

- [Running Iceberg in production: file sizes, object-storage paths, and the jobs you must schedule](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergProductionGuide/): The settings that decide whether an Iceberg table stays fast are set at create time and enforced by jobs nobody schedules. Here is what target file size actually does, what object-storage paths look like when enabled, and the maintenance that turns a working table into one that keeps working.
- [Migrating Hive tables to Iceberg: snapshot first, migrate second](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergHiveMigration/): Two procedures convert a Hive table to Iceberg without moving data. One makes a parallel copy you can test against while the original keeps serving; the other converts in place and is hard to undo. Here is what each does, and the catalog requirement that decides whether either works.
- [CDC into Iceberg: the delete files nobody counted](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergCdcPipelines/): A change stream landing in an Iceberg table with MERGE INTO works on day one and degrades quietly after that. Three merges added three delete files and 960 dead records while the row count barely moved. Here is the accounting, and the job that pays it back.
- [Time travel and rollback in Iceberg: undoing a bad write in one statement](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergTimeTravel/): Every Iceberg commit leaves a snapshot, so reading the table as it was is a query and undoing a bad write is a procedure call. A rollback took a table from 5 rows back to 3, and the history table kept a record of the snapshot that was abandoned.
- [Copy-on-write or merge-on-read: choosing how an Iceberg table pays for a delete](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergCopyOnWriteMergeOnRead/): An Iceberg table can rewrite whole data files when you delete a row, or write a small delete file and merge it at read time. The same DELETE produced two completely different file layouts and two different snapshot operations. Here is what each costs, and which workloads want which.
- [Streaming into Iceberg: availableNow, checkpoints, and the snapshot count nobody watches](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergStreamingIngestion/): A streaming write into Iceberg commits a snapshot per micro-batch, so the trigger you choose decides how fast your metadata grows. Here is what availableNow actually does, why re-running it changes nothing, and the accounting that makes a streaming table slow down over weeks.
- [Loading data into Iceberg: appends, overwrites and row-level SQL](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergIngestion/): Iceberg accepts data four ways and each leaves a different mark in the snapshot log. A MERGE applying a changelog produced inserts, updates and deletes in one statement and recorded it as a single overwrite snapshot.
- [Hidden partitioning and partition evolution: changing layout without rewriting history](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergPartitioning/): Iceberg derives partition values from a transform on a real column, so queries never name the partition. That indirection is also what lets the layout change later: after switching months to days, two of three data files still carried the old spec and nothing was rewritten.
- [Schema evolution in Iceberg: why a rename costs nothing](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergSchemaEvolution/): Renaming a column in an Iceberg table rewrote no data and kept the column's field id. That identifier is the whole mechanism, and it is why schema changes here do not have the failure modes they have on Hive tables.
- [Iceberg format versions: what v1, v2, v3 and v4 actually change](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergFormatVersions/): The format version decides whether a table can delete a row without rewriting a file, and whether every row carries an identity. All four versions were created and written against the same engine. Here is what each adds and what upgrading costs.
- [Iceberg catalogs: the one pointer that makes a table a table](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergCatalogs/): A catalog answers one question — which metadata file is current — and how it answers decides whether concurrent writers are safe. The choice even changes the filenames on disk, which is why Iceberg tutorials describe the metadata directory in contradictory ways.
- [Life of a write query in Iceberg: three files, one pointer swap, and what ACID means here](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergWritePath/): Every Iceberg commit writes a manifest, a manifest list and a metadata file, then swaps one pointer. Two writers hammering the same table produced a linear snapshot chain with no lost rows and no errors. Here is the sequence, and what optimistic concurrency actually does.
- [Life of a read query in Iceberg: four prunes before a byte of data is read](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergReadPath/): Planning an Iceberg query is a sequence of eliminations against metadata. Each level discards work the next level would have done, and the last one only works if your data is sorted. Here is each step with the metadata it reads.
- [The three tiers of an Iceberg table: catalog, metadata, data](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergThreeTierArchitecture/): An Iceberg table is three layers with one job each: a pointer, a tree that describes files, and the files. Knowing which layer a problem lives in is most of operating one, because each has its own growth rate and its own maintenance job.
- [A local Iceberg playground: Spark, MinIO and a REST catalog in one compose file](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergLocalPlayground/): A working Iceberg environment on a laptop needs three things that have to agree with each other: object storage, a catalog, and an engine. Here is a compose file that brings up all three, the configuration that makes Spark talk to them, and what the table looks like in object storage afterwards.
- [What Hive tables could not do, and why Iceberg exists](https://rangareddy.github.io/WhyIcebergExists/): A Hive table is a directory, and every limitation follows from that. Iceberg replaces the directory with a metadata tree that names every file. Here is what that changes, from atomic commits to schema changes that do not rewrite data.
- [Running Iceberg on Apache Polaris: one compose file, two storage backends](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkIcebergPolaris/): A working Spark and Iceberg setup on Apache Polaris in four steps: one compose file, one provisioning script, one Spark launch, and the same SQL against both a local directory and MinIO. Every command was run, and the errors worth knowing are collected at the end rather than scattered through.
- [Apache Iceberg architecture: what actually happens when you commit](https://rangareddy.github.io/ApacheIcebergArchitecture/): A walk through the Iceberg metadata tree from a catalog pointer down to a single data file: what a commit actually swaps, how planning prunes before it reads, and why the catalog is part of the table.
- [Apache Iceberg on Spark: the complete cheat sheet](https://rangareddy.github.io/ApacheIcebergCheatSheet/): One page to keep open while you work: the snapshot tree, metadata tables, hidden partitioning, row-level operation modes, branches and tags, the twenty CALL procedures and the maintenance jobs, with the property and default for each.

## Lakehouse

- [Run every demo on this blog locally: one compose stack for Hudi, Iceberg and Delta](https://rangareddy.github.io/DatalakeDockerDemos/): The measurements in these posts came from a local stack rather than a cloud account. Here is that stack, the one command that starts it, and the demo scripts that reproduce each post's numbers on your own machine.
- [One table, three formats: Iceberg, Delta and Hudi interoperability](https://rangareddy.github.io/IcebergInteroperability/): Iceberg, Delta and Hudi all describe Parquet files with metadata. That shared substrate is what lets a table be readable as more than one format without copying data — and it is also where the limits of that trick live.
- [Table maintenance for Iceberg and Hudi: compaction, expiry, and the space you did not reclaim](https://rangareddy.github.io/TableMaintenance/): Compaction rewrites small files into large ones and reclaims nothing. The old files stay on disk, still referenced, until a separate expiry or cleaning job removes them. Here is what each maintenance operation does to an Iceberg and a Hudi table, measured file by file.
- [Apache XTable cheat sheet: one table, every format](https://rangareddy.github.io/ApacheXTableCheatSheet/): One page to keep open while you work: what XTable converts, where the metadata lands, the build, the config file, every RunSync flag, catalog registration and the engine matrix.
- [Open table formats in practice: what actually differs between Iceberg, Hudi and Delta Lake](https://rangareddy.github.io/OpenTableFormats/): All three formats give you ACID commits, time travel and schema evolution, so a feature checklist will not tell you which to pick. What separates them is how each one tracks table state, how each one applies a row-level update, and what each one asks you to operate.
- [Apache XTable incremental sync: how to keep your conversions fast](https://rangareddy.github.io/XTableIncrementalSync/): XTable exposes one Hudi, Iceberg or Delta table as the other two by writing metadata rather than copying data. It picks FULL or INCREMENTAL per target format on every run, and one setting on your side keeps it on the fast path. Here is how the decision works, from source, and how to confirm it in the log.

## Linux

- [Kerberos Setup in Linux](https://rangareddy.github.io/KerberoSetup/): Install and configure a Kerberos KDC and its clients on Linux end to end: kdc.conf, krb5.conf, the KDC database, ACLs, the admin principal, keytabs and a test from both server and client.

## Spark

- [Structured Streaming internals: the checkpoint, the state store, and what a restart cannot change](https://rangareddy.github.io/StructuredStreamingInternals/): A streaming query is a loop that writes what it is about to do, does it, then writes that it finished. Here is what that loop puts on disk, how the state store is laid out underneath it, why the watermark lives in two files, and which settings become permanent the first time the query runs.
- [Spark performance tuning: seventeen techniques, and how to prove each one worked](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkPerformanceOptimization/): Most Spark tuning advice is a list of settings with no way to tell whether any of them fired. These seventeen techniques each come with the code, the evidence that the optimization applied, and the failure mode that silently turns it off again.
- [Spark shuffle internals: the three writers, and which one your job gets](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkShuffleInternals/): Spark has three shuffle writers and chooses one per shuffle without ever naming the choice. Here is that decision tree read from the source and confirmed by running it, what lands on disk, what the reduce side does with it, who serves the files when an executor dies, and how to avoid the shuffle altogether.
- [Accelerating Spark queries with Apache DataFusion Comet](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkDataFusionComet/): Comet replaces Spark's JVM operators with vectorized native ones built on Arrow and DataFusion, without changing your query. Here is what it swaps, the configuration that turns it on, how to read the plan to prove it worked, and what happens to the operators it cannot run.
- [Spark Submit Command generator using Iceberg Catalog](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkIcebergSubmitCommand/): Pick a catalog type (Hive, Hadoop, REST or JDBC) plus Spark, Iceberg and Scala versions, and get the spark-shell command with the right iceberg-spark-runtime coordinates and catalog configs. Every version pair comes from the Iceberg release's own build rather than a hand-kept table.
- [Spark Shuffle Partition Generator tool](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkShufflePartitionGenerator/): Enter the shuffle input size, executor count and cores per executor, and get a spark.sql.shuffle.partitions value back, sized so each partition stays inside the range Spark handles well rather than left at the default 200.
- [Spark Submit Command Formatter tool](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkSubmitFormatter/): Paste a spark-submit command and get it back formatted across lines or minified onto one line, with every Spark option resolved to the configuration property it sets and your application's own arguments kept separate.
- [Spark Configuration Generator tool](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkConfigurationGenerator/): Enter the node count, cores per node and memory per node for your cluster and get back executor count, executor cores, executor memory and memory overhead, ready to paste into spark-shell.
- [Logging a Spark stream: the job you cannot restart to debug](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkStreamingCustomLogging/): A Structured Streaming query logs every micro-batch for as long as it runs, so the volume tracks partition count rather than data volume, and you cannot restart the job to raise a level. Here is the Log4j 2 config that bounds it, the live reconfiguration that avoids the restart, and the Log4j 1 equivalents.
- [Every Apache Spark release, and the problem each one was built to solve](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkReleaseHistory/): A release-by-release walk through Spark's history, from the research releases to the current line: the theory behind what each version added, which defaults it changed under you, what it deleted, and a runnable example for the features that matter. Every example run against a live cluster rather than recalled.
- [Spark memory management: every region, and the arithmetic that sizes it](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkMemoryManagement/): An executor's memory is four regions inside the heap plus two outside it, and the sizes follow from three numbers. Here is the arithmetic, checked against a running executor, the elastic boundary read from the source, what the binary row format is measured to save, where PySpark's workers actually live, and how to tell which of the three layers killed your job.
- [Adaptive query execution in Apache Spark: what it re-plans, and what it leaves alone](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkAQE/): Adaptive execution re-plans a query while it runs, using measured shuffle sizes instead of estimates. Here is each thing it changes, shown as a before and after plan, the thresholds that decide whether it fires, and the parts of the plan it never revisits.
- [Data skew in Apache Spark: how to see it, and nine ways to fix it](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkDataSkew/): One key holding most of the rows turns a parallel job into a serial one. Here is how to measure skew rather than guess at it, and nine fixes with the partition distributions and correctness checks for each, from salting to letting adaptive execution split the partition for you.
- [Inside Spark's Catalyst optimizer: how a query gets rewritten, rule by rule](https://rangareddy.github.io/CatalystOptimizer/): Catalyst is a tree-rewriting engine, not a black box. The four-phase pipeline, what a rule is in the source, rule-based versus cost-based optimization with the statistics to prove the difference, physical planning, Tungsten codegen, dynamic partition pruning and adaptive execution, all read out of Spark's own instrumentation.
- [Apache Iceberg through Spark Connect: the full surface, and the extension that breaks time travel](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkConnectIceberg/): Iceberg's whole write and read surface works from a Spark Connect client that has no jars installed, including MERGE, metadata tables, procedures and time travel. One thing breaks it, and it is not Spark Connect: loading Hudi's session extension alongside Iceberg's.
- [Apache Hudi through Spark Connect: running the full table surface from a thin client](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkConnectHudi/): Spark Connect splits the driver in two, which changes where Hudi has to be installed. Here is how to run a server that speaks Hudi, every operation that works from a client with no jars, and the four that do not, each one run rather than assumed.
- [Apache Spark joins in depth: the five strategies and how one gets picked](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkJoinsInDepth/): Spark has five join strategies and one decision procedure that chooses between them. Here is how each works, the exact order Spark tries them in, which join types quietly forbid which strategy, and what to do per scenario.
- [200 Apache Spark interview questions, with answers](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkInterviewQuestions/): Two hundred questions from first principles to production scenarios, each answered in depth with the mechanism, an example and the trap. Grouped by topic and collapsed, so you can drill one section at a time.
- [Apache Spark architecture: what actually happens when you call an action](https://rangareddy.github.io/ApacheSparkArchitecture/): A walk through the Spark runtime from the driver down to a single task: who schedules what, where memory goes, how a shuffle is written, and which class to read when a job misbehaves.
- [Apache Spark: the complete cheat sheet](https://rangareddy.github.io/ApacheSparkCheatSheet/): One page to keep open while you work: the execution model, spark-submit, the memory split, join strategies, shuffle and partitioning, adaptive query execution, caching, streaming and the configs that matter, with the default and the version for each.
- [A Spark JVM playbook: custom logging, class loading, stack size and proxies](https://rangareddy.github.io/SparkTroubleshootingPlaybook/): Four techniques that pay for themselves on nearly every Spark investigation: swap in a custom Log4j 2 config, trace class loading, raise the JVM stack size, and route traffic through an HTTP proxy. All four go through the same two configs, so learning one teaches you the rest.

## Tools

- [Inspecting Parquet files from the command line with parquet-cli](https://rangareddy.github.io/ParquetTools/): parquet-cli is the maintained command-line tool for Parquet, and it does more than parquet-tools ever did. Here is the command-for-command migration, every transcript captured from a real run, plus what to know about rewrite.
